title: Module 2: A Short History — From Calipers to Coordinates
text:
Stage 1: Typology and Description (19th–early 20th century)
The earliest approach to artefact shape was pure description: “This is a Type IIb axe.” Typologies classified objects into categories based on a researcher’s judgment of meaningful shape features.
The strengths: Fast, accessible, connects to cultural history.
The weaknesses: - Different researchers draw type boundaries differently - Impossible to test: how different do two shapes have to be to belong to different types? - Loses gradational variation: what about the object that sits between two types?
Typology is not wrong — it is still useful. But it is qualitative and subjective.

title: Module 2: A Short History — From Calipers to Coordinates
text:
Stage 2: Traditional (Multivariate) Morphometrics (1960s–1980s)
The response was to measure objects with calipers and treat the measurements statistically. Length, width, height, diameter, ratio of length to width — these are traditional morphometric variables.
Multivariate statistics (PCA, discriminant analysis, cluster analysis) were applied to these measurements.
The improvement: Objective, reproducible, testable.
The remaining problem: Which measurements to take? Measurements depend on the researcher’s choice. They also lose geometric information: knowing the length and width of a coin doesn’t tell you the shape of the portrait.

title: Module 2: A Short History — From Calipers to Coordinates
text:
Stage 3: The Morphometric Revolution (1980s–1990s)
A group of biologists and statisticians — David Kendall, Fred Bookstein, F. James Rohlf, and others — developed a fundamentally new approach: instead of measuring distances between landmarks, record the coordinates of the landmarks themselves.
This seems like a small change but has profound consequences: - The full geometry of the configuration is preserved - All specimens can be brought into a common coordinate system (Procrustes alignment) - Shape can be visualized as continuous deformation - The mathematics is rigorous and well-understood
This is geometric morphometrics.

title: Module 2: A Short History — From Calipers to Coordinates
section: The Three Data Types in GM
text:
The Three Data Types in GM

Type 1: Landmarks
A landmark is a discrete, identifiable point that corresponds to the same location across all specimens in the study.
There are three classical types (Bookstein 1991):








Type
Definition
Example on a coin




Type I
Biologically/archaeologically meaningful intersection point
Corner of die border at 12 o’clock


Type II
Point of maximum curvature or extremum
Tip of portrait nose


Type III
Constructed from other points
Midpoint of the coin diameter









The Homology Problem



A landmark must correspond to the same location in all specimens — not just geometrically similar, but biologically or archaeologically homologous. This is the hardest conceptual problem in landmark GM.
On a coin: is the “corner of the chin” always the same point across portraits of different emperors? This requires archaeological judgment, not just geometry.


When to use landmarks: Objects with discrete, identifiable reference points. Coins with portrait features, skulls, arrowheads with defined tip/base/notch points.



Type 2: Semi-Landmarks
Semi-landmarks are placed along curves where there are no discrete homologous points. They are allowed to “slide” along the curve during analysis to minimize bending energy.
When to use: Curved outlines of objects like pots or axes, where there is no single identifiable point but you want to capture the curve geometry.



Type 3: Outlines
An outline is a complete contour of the object — a closed curve represented as a sequence of \((x, y)\) coordinates.
Unlike landmarks, outlines don’t require you to identify specific homologous points. Instead, the outline is decomposed mathematically into a series of components using Elliptic Fourier Analysis (EFA).
When to use: Smooth, rounded objects without clear landmark points — pottery profiles, axe outlines, coins (as a simpler alternative to portrait landmarks).

title: Module 7: Case Study I — Roman Coins and Imperial Standardization
text:
The Roman Empire produced coins at a scale that no earlier civilization had matched. In the 2nd century CE alone, hundreds of millions of denarii were struck across the empire. Every coin bore the portrait of the reigning emperor — a face seen by nearly everyone in the Roman world.
Coins were not just money. They were propaganda: images of imperial power circulating to the edges of the known world. The obverse portrait was a deliberate political statement. Die-cutters at the imperial mint were artisans who worked within strict iconographic conventions.



Hadrian (r. 117–138 CE) - Known for traveling the empire, fortifying its borders (Hadrian’s Wall) - Iconic portraiture: philosophical beard, often shown with idealized Greek features - Reformed the coinage: new portrait types introduced at different points in his reign
Antoninus Pius (r. 138–161 CE) - Succeeded Hadrian; reign known for stability - Portrait more Roman in character: clean-shaven early, then bearded - Some of the most artistically refined denarii in the Imperial sequence



Do coins of Hadrian and Antoninus Pius cluster separately in shape space?
Sub-questions: - Is the shape difference between the emperors larger than the variation within each reign? - Which specific shape features (captured by which PCs) best separate the two groups? - What does any difference — or similarity — tell us about mint standardization?

Step 4: Statistical test — permutation MANOVA
from scipy.spatial.distance import cdist
from scipy.stats import f

def permutation_manova(scores, labels, n_perm=999, n_pcs=5):
    """
    Permutation-based MANOVA on PC scores.
    Tests whether group centroids differ more than expected by chance.
    """
    X = scores[:, :n_pcs]
    labels = np.array(labels)
    groups = np.unique(labels)

    # Observed F-statistic (ratio of between-group to within-group variance)
    grand_mean = X.mean(axis=0)
    ss_between = sum(
        (X[labels == g].mean(axis=0) - grand_mean)**2 * (labels == g).sum()
        for g in groups
    ).sum()
    ss_within = sum(
        ((X[labels == g] - X[labels == g].mean(axis=0))**2).sum()
        for g in groups
    )
    n, k = len(labels), len(groups)
    f_obs = (ss_between / (k - 1)) / (ss_within / (n - k))

    # Permutation distribution
    f_perm = []
    for _ in range(n_perm):
        perm_labels = np.random.permutation(labels)
        ss_b = sum(
            (X[perm_labels == g].mean(axis=0) - grand_mean)**2 * (perm_labels == g).sum()
            for g in groups
        ).sum()
        ss_w = sum(
            ((X[perm_labels == g] - X[perm_labels == g].mean(axis=0))**2).sum()
            for g in groups
        )
        f_perm.append((ss_b / (k - 1)) / (ss_w / (n - k)))

    p_value = (np.sum(np.array(f_perm) >= f_obs) + 1) / (n_perm + 1)
    return f_obs, p_value

f_stat, p_val = permutation_manova(scores, labels)
print(f"Permutation MANOVA: F = {f_stat:.3f}, p = {p_val:.3f}")

title: Module 7: Case Study I — Roman Coins and Imperial Standardization
text:
Interpreting the Results

If the groups separate:
The two emperors’ coins occupy different regions of shape space. This could indicate: - Portrait style was deliberately differentiated by reign - Die-cutters changed their conventions between reigns - Different workshops produced the two series


If the groups overlap substantially:
Shape variation within each reign is larger than variation between reigns. This could indicate: - Consistent mint conventions that persisted across reigns - Strong iconographic standards imposed by the central mint - Our landmark protocol doesn’t capture the features that actually differ


Neither outcome is “wrong”:
Both tell us something real about Roman mint organization.

title: Module 7: Case Study I — Roman Coins and Imperial Standardization
section: Discussion: What Shape Can and Cannot Tell Us
text:
Discussion: What Shape Can and Cannot Tell Us
Shape analysis of coins has real limitations:

We can only measure what we digitize. If portrait style differs in surface detail (texture, modelling depth) but not in overall proportion, landmark analysis misses it.
Die variation within a reign is large. Many different pairs of dies were used for each emperor. Is our sample large enough to characterize each reign’s “typical” shape?
What counts as the same “type”? Hadrian’s portraiture changed significantly over his long reign. Should we subdivide by portrait type before comparing?

These are not reasons to dismiss GM — they are reasons to design studies carefully and interpret results with appropriate caution.

title: Module 6: PCA — Exploring the Shape Space
text:
After Procrustes alignment, each coin exists as a point in a 12-dimensional shape space. We cannot visualize 12 dimensions. Principal Components Analysis (PCA) solves this.
PCA finds the directions in shape space that capture the most variation. The first principal component (PC1) is the single axis that explains the most shape variation in the dataset. PC2 explains the most of what is left, and so on.

title: Module 6: PCA — Exploring the Shape Space
text:
What PCA Is (Conceptually)
Imagine all your coins lying in a cloud of points in shape space. PCA finds the longest axis through this cloud (PC1), then the longest axis perpendicular to that (PC2), and so on.
By plotting PC1 vs. PC2, we capture the majority of shape variation in two dimensions we can see.






What PC scores mean



Each specimen gets a score on each PC axis. A high positive score on PC1 means the specimen has a lot of the shape variation described by PC1 (in the positive direction). A near-zero score means the specimen is close to the mean shape on that axis.

title: Module 6: PCA — Exploring the Shape Space
text:
Shape Deformation Grids
The most powerful tool for interpreting PCA results is the thin-plate spline deformation grid.
A deformation grid shows how the mean shape must be deformed to produce the shape at any point in shape space. It is a visual map of the geometric transformation between two shapes.
Reading a deformation grid: - Regions where the grid is compressed → relative contraction toward the target shape - Regions where the grid is stretched → relative expansion toward the target shape - Grid lines that curve sharply → strong local deformation
We generate deformation grids using the morphops thin-plate spline functions.

title: Module 8: Outline Analysis — Elliptic Fourier Analysis
section: The Core Idea: Decomposing a Shape
text:
The Core Idea: Decomposing a Shape
EFA treats an outline as a mathematical function and decomposes it into a sum of simpler components — elliptic harmonics — in exactly the same way that a complex musical chord can be decomposed into individual sine waves (Fourier analysis).

The Musical Analogy

A musical note is a complex wave
Fourier analysis breaks it into pure sine waves at different frequencies
Low frequencies = the overall character of the sound
High frequencies = fine detail and texture

For outlines: - 1st harmonic = the overall elliptical shape (elongated vs. round) - 2nd–4th harmonics = major proportional features (where is the widest point? how asymmetric is the base?) - Higher harmonics = finer details (edge serrations, small bumps)

title: Module 8: Outline Analysis — Elliptic Fourier Analysis
text:
How EFA Works
An outline is represented as a closed sequence of \((x_i, y_i)\) coordinates. EFA decomposes the \(x\) and \(y\) coordinates separately as Fourier series, then recombines them as ellipses.
Each harmonic \(n\) produces 4 coefficients: \((a_n, b_n, c_n, d_n)\).
For \(N\) harmonics, we get \(4N\) coefficients total. These coefficients are the shape — they can be used directly in PCA just like landmark coordinates.

Normalization
EFA coefficients must be normalized to remove the effects of size, position, rotation, and starting point. After normalization, only shape information remains.


Choosing N (number of harmonics)
More harmonics = more detail captured, but also more noise. The standard criterion:

Choose the minimum \(N\) that explains ≥ 99% of the outline shape variation in your sample.

For axes like ours, 8–12 harmonics is typically sufficient.

Step 1: Load and preprocess one axe image

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from skimage import io, color, filters, measure
import pyefd

def extract_outline(image_path, threshold_method='otsu'):
    """
    Load an axe image and extract its largest outline contour.
    Returns: array of (x, y) coordinates
    """
    img = io.imread(image_path, as_gray=True)

    # Threshold to binary
    thresh = filters.threshold_otsu(img)
    binary = img > thresh  # background = True, object = False

    # Find contours of the object
    contours = measure.find_contours(~binary, 0.5)

    # Keep the largest contour (= the axe)
    largest = max(contours, key=len)
    return largest  # shape: (n_points, 2)

# Test on one axe
outline = extract_outline("data/flanged_axes/G3/ALT.tif")
print(f"Outline has {len(outline)} points")

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 8))
plt.plot(outline[:, 1], -outline[:, 0], 'b-', linewidth=1)
plt.fill(outline[:, 1], -outline[:, 0], alpha=0.2)
plt.title("ALT axe outline")
plt.axis('equal')
plt.show()


Step 2: Fit EFA
# Fit EFA with 12 harmonics, normalized
coeffs = pyefd.elliptic_fourier_descriptors(
    outline, order=12, normalize=True
)
print(f"EFA coefficients shape: {coeffs.shape}")  # (12, 4)
# Each row = one harmonic: (a_n, b_n, c_n, d_n)


Step 3: Reconstruct the shape from EFA (sanity check)
# Reconstruct the outline from EFA coefficients (should match original)
locus = pyefd.reconstruct_contour(coeffs, num_points=300)

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 8))
plt.plot(outline[:, 1], -outline[:, 0], 'gray', linewidth=2, alpha=0.5, label='Original')
plt.plot(locus[:, 0], -locus[:, 1], 'r-', linewidth=2, label='EFA reconstruction')
plt.legend()
plt.axis('equal')
plt.title("EFA reconstruction (12 harmonics)")
plt.show()


Step 4: Process all axes and stack into a matrix
import os

def process_all_axes(folder_g3, folder_g4):
    """Load all axe images, extract outlines, and fit EFA."""
    all_coeffs = []
    all_labels = []
    all_names = []

    for folder, group in [(folder_g3, 'G3'), (folder_g4, 'G4')]:
        for fname in sorted(os.listdir(folder)):
            if fname.endswith('.tif'):
                path = os.path.join(folder, fname)
                try:
                    outline = extract_outline(path)
                    coeffs = pyefd.elliptic_fourier_descriptors(
                        outline, order=12, normalize=True
                    )
                    # Flatten: 12 harmonics × 4 coefficients = 48 values
                    all_coeffs.append(coeffs.flatten())
                    all_labels.append(group)
                    all_names.append(fname.replace('.tif', ''))
                except Exception as e:
                    print(f"Skipped {fname}: {e}")

    return np.array(all_coeffs), np.array(all_labels), np.array(all_names)

coeff_matrix, labels, names = process_all_axes(
    "data/flanged_axes/G3/",
    "data/flanged_axes/G4/"
)
print(f"Matrix shape: {coeff_matrix.shape}")
# Expected: (n_axes, 48)
print(f"Groups: {dict(zip(*np.unique(labels, return_counts=True)))}")


Step 5: PCA on EFA coefficients
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import pandas as pd

pca = PCA()
scores = pca.fit_transform(coeff_matrix)
var_exp = pca.explained_variance_ratio_ * 100

df = pd.DataFrame({
    'PC1': scores[:, 0],
    'PC2': scores[:, 1],
    'Group': labels,
    'Name': names
})

# Plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
colors = {'G3': '#1976D2', 'G4': '#C62828'}

for group, grp_df in df.groupby('Group'):
    ax.scatter(grp_df['PC1'], grp_df['PC2'],
               color=colors[group], label=group,
               s=60, alpha=0.85, edgecolor='white')

ax.set_xlabel(f"PC1 ({var_exp[0]:.1f}%)")
ax.set_ylabel(f"PC2 ({var_exp[1]:.1f}%)")
ax.set_title("EFA Shape Space: Bronze Age Flanged Axes")
ax.legend(title="Typological Group")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Unlike landmark PCA, EFA PCA axes don’t directly map to shifts in specific landmark positions. Instead, we visualize the reconstructed outlines at the extremes of each PC:
# Reconstruct mean shape and ±2SD shapes along PC1
mean_coeffs = pca.mean_.reshape(12, 4)
pc1_vector  = pca.components_[0].reshape(12, 4)
std1        = np.sqrt(pca.explained_variance_[0])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 7))
for ax, scale, title in zip(axes, [-2, 0, 2], ['PC1 min (−2SD)', 'Mean shape', 'PC1 max (+2SD)']):
    shape_coeffs = mean_coeffs + scale * std1 * pc1_vector
    locus = pyefd.reconstruct_contour(shape_coeffs, num_points=400)
    ax.fill(locus[:, 0], locus[:, 1], alpha=0.3, color='steelblue')
    ax.plot(locus[:, 0], locus[:, 1], 'steelblue', linewidth=2)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_aspect('equal')
    ax.axis('off')

plt.suptitle("Shape variation along PC1 — Bronze Age Axes", fontsize=13)

plt.show()

text:
Every object ever made by human hands has a shape. Archaeologists have always described shape — “biconical,” “carinated,” “leaf-shaped” — but what if we could measure it? What if we could compare the shapes of hundreds of objects objectively, statistically, and reproducibly?
That is what geometric morphometrics (GM) does.

title: Module 1: What Is Shape? Why Does It Matter?
section: Size vs. Shape: The Fundamental Distinction
text:
Size vs. Shape: The Fundamental Distinction
The most important concept in this course is the difference between size and shape.






Kendall’s Definition (1977)



Shape is “all the geometric information that remains when location, scale and rotation effects are filtered out from an object.”
In other words: shape is what’s left when you remove where it is, how big it is, and which way it’s pointing.


Think of a wine bottle. Two bottles can have the same shape but be different sizes (a regular bottle vs. a magnum). Two bottles can be the same size but different shapes (Bordeaux vs. Burgundy style). We are interested in shape — independent of size.
For archaeology, this distinction is fundamental: - A Roman denarius from mint A and mint B might weigh the same (same size) but have subtly different portrait proportions (different shape) - Two Bronze Age axes from different regions might be the same length (same size) but have different blade geometries (different shape)

title: Module 1: What Is Shape? Why Does It Matter?
text:
What Shape Can Tell Us
Shape in archaeological objects is not accidental. It encodes:







Signal
Example




Technological tradition
Bronze Age axes made by the same tradition share outline shape


Chronological change
Coin portrait conventions evolved over time — shape records this


Regional identity
Pottery production traditions leave shape signatures


Function
Storage jars have different shape profiles than cooking pots


Exchange and copying
Imitated objects share shape with their originals


Standardization
Mass-produced objects (coins) show low shape variation when quality control was high

title: Module 1: What Is Shape? Why Does It Matter?
section: Three Case Studies We Will Explore
text:
Three Case Studies We Will Explore

1. Roman Imperial Coins


Roman denarii of Hadrian (r. 117–138 CE) and Antoninus Pius (r. 138–161 CE).
The question: did Roman die-cutters maintain consistent shape standards? Can we detect differences between emperors’ coinages from shape alone?
The Roman Empire produced coins in enormous quantities. Die-cutters were skilled artisans working under imperial oversight. Every coin was intended to look the same — but did they? And if there are subtle shape differences, what do they mean?



2. European Bronze Age Flanged Axes
Bronze Age metalworkers cast flanged axes according to visual templates — there were no written instructions, no blueprints. Shape was transmitted through apprenticeship and observation.
The dataset includes two typological groups (G3 and G4) from across Central Europe. The question: do these typological groups reflect genuine morphological distinctions, or is shape variation continuous? And can we detect regional craft traditions from shape alone?



3. Ancient Pottery
Pottery is the most common archaeological find almost everywhere in the world. Its shape reflects the potter’s training, the community’s traditions, the vessel’s function, and the period of production.
The pottery dataset (published open-access 2023–2025) will let us ask: can we identify production traditions or chronological periods purely from outline shape?

title: Module 1: What Is Shape? Why Does It Matter?
text:
Traditional Morphometrics vs. Geometric Morphometrics
Before GM, archaeologists measured objects with calipers: length, width, height, diameter. These measurements are called traditional morphometrics or multivariate morphometrics.
The problem: measurements depend on where you put the caliper. They don’t capture shape — they capture specific distances that may or may not represent the shape differences you care about.
GM solves this by working directly with coordinates — the \((x, y)\) positions of specific points on the object. This captures the full geometry of the shape, not just a few distances.







Traditional Morphometrics
Geometric Morphometrics




Distances and ratios
Coordinates of points


Loses geometric information
Preserves full geometry


Hard to visualize
Visualization via deformation grids


No standard alignment
Procrustes alignment removes size/position/rotation


Many variables, unclear meaning
Shape as a single multivariate variable

The Three Methods We Will Use

1. Landmark Analysis
Place discrete points — landmarks — at biologically or archaeologically meaningful locations on the object. This is the main method for the coin analysis.


2. Outline Analysis (Elliptic Fourier Analysis)
Trace the outline (contour) of the object and decompose it into mathematical functions. This is the main method for the flanged axes and pottery.


3. 3D Morphometrics (Week 11 overview)
Extend landmarks and surfaces into three dimensions using photogrammetry or scanning. We will not do a full 3D analysis but will understand the principles.

text:
Last week, you saw the raw coin landmarks scattered across the plot. Each coin image was scanned at a different size, with the coin in a different position and orientation. Before we can compare shapes, we need to remove these irrelevant differences.
Procrustes alignment is the mathematical solution.

title: Module 5: Procrustes Alignment — Putting Shapes in the Same Space
text:
What GPA Does: Three Steps
Generalized Procrustes Analysis (GPA) removes three sources of non-shape variation:

Step 1: Translation
Move every configuration so its centroid (geometric center) sits at the origin \((0, 0)\).


Step 2: Scaling
Resize every configuration so its centroid size equals 1.
Centroid size = the square root of the sum of squared distances from each landmark to the centroid:
\[CS = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{k} d_i^2}\]
where \(d_i\) is the distance from landmark \(i\) to the centroid.
This is the standard size measure in GM because it is statistically independent of shape (unlike length or width, which are correlated with shape).


Step 3: Rotation
Rotate each configuration to minimize the total squared distance between its landmarks and the mean configuration (consensus shape).
After all three steps, all configurations are superimposed in the same coordinate system. What remains is shape.

title: Module 5: Procrustes Alignment — Putting Shapes in the Same Space
text:
The Consensus Shape
After GPA, we can calculate the mean shape (consensus) — the average position of each landmark across all aligned specimens. This is our reference shape for visualization.
Shape variation in the dataset is then measured as deviations from this consensus.

What Does Centroid Size Tell Us?
Centroid size is a by-product of GPA. It tells us about the relative size of each specimen. We can ask:

Is size correlated with shape? (This is called allometry)
Were some coins produced from larger flans than others?
Did coin size change over time?

section: A Visual Intuition for Shape Space
text:
A Visual Intuition for Shape Space
After GPA, all configurations exist in a high-dimensional shape space (Kendall’s shape space). Each specimen is a single point in this space.
The dimensions of shape space = (number of landmarks × 2) − 4 for 2D data (We subtract 4 for the 2 translation, 1 scale, and 1 rotation degrees of freedom removed by GPA.)
For our 8-landmark coin dataset: \((8 \times 2) - 4 = 12\) dimensions.
Twelve dimensions is too many to visualize directly. That is what PCA is for — next week.

Week 8: Outline Analysis — Elliptic Fourier Analysis
Lecture (90 min):

When landmarks aren’t enough: objects without discrete homologous points
What an outline is: a closed contour captured as a sequence of x,y coordinates
Elliptic Fourier Analysis: decomposing an outline into a sum of elliptic harmonics

Analogy: like breaking down a musical chord into individual notes
The first harmonic captures basic size/shape; higher harmonics add detail

Choosing the number of harmonics: the variance explained criterion
Normalizing for size, position, rotation, and starting point
How EFA + PCA gives us the same kind of shape space as landmark GM

text:
Why We Digitize
Before we can analyze shapes statistically, we need to capture them as coordinates. The process of placing landmark points on images and recording their \((x, y)\) positions is called digitizing.
The quality of every downstream analysis depends entirely on the quality of digitizing. Sloppy landmark placement = unreliable results. This is why we spend a full week on it.

title: Module 3: Seeing Shape — Digitizing Landmarks
text:
Image Preparation
Good digitizing starts with good images. The requirements:

Scale Bar
Every image must have a scale bar — a line of known length that lets you convert pixel distances to real-world measurements. Without a scale bar, you can compare shapes but not sizes.
The coin images in our dataset have scale bars embedded. The axe images in our dataset are calibrated via the TPS file metadata.


Orientation Convention
All specimens must be oriented the same way before digitizing. For coins: portrait facing right, die axis vertical. For axes: blade pointing down, flat face toward the viewer.
Inconsistent orientation is corrected by Procrustes alignment — but it’s still good practice to standardize before digitizing.


Image Quality

Sufficient resolution to place landmarks accurately
Consistent lighting (shadows create false edges)
Clean background (no visual noise near the object outline)

One of the most important exercises in any GM study is quantifying inter-observer error — how much do two different digitizers disagree on landmark placement?

title: Module 9: Case Study II — Bronze Age Axes and Craft Networks
text:
The Bronze Age in Europe (c. 2300–800 BCE) was defined by metallurgy. Bronze — an alloy of copper and tin — required long-distance exchange networks, because copper and tin deposits are rarely found together. The very existence of Bronze Age material culture implies connectivity.
Flanged axes are among the most common Bronze Age metal finds. They were functional tools (woodworking, combat) but also prestige objects, hoarded in deposits, and possibly used as currency-like valuables.
The “flanged” design — raised ridges along the sides to help hafting — was a technological solution that spread across Europe in the Middle Bronze Age. But how did this spread happen?



Our dataset comes from Central European flanged axes classified into two typological groups (designations following standard Bronze Age typo-chronology):

G3: Earlier group, c. 1600–1400 BCE. Primarily found in western Central Europe.
G4: Later group, c. 1400–1200 BCE. Wider geographic distribution.

Traditional typology classifies them by a combination of proportions (flange height, blade width relative to total length) and decorative features. But typology is always a simplification.
The question: does shape variation in these axes respect the G3/G4 boundary? Is there a continuous morphological gradient? Are there regional variants within each group?

title: Module 9: Case Study II — Bronze Age Axes and Craft Networks
text:
Why This Matters Historically
Three possible outcomes:

Outcome A: Clean separation
G3 and G4 form distinct, non-overlapping clusters in shape space. This supports the idea that each group represents a coherent production tradition — perhaps a specific workshop, region, or period with its own design template.
Implication: Bronze Age metalworkers maintained strict shape standards within each tradition, possibly through apprenticeship networks with limited cross-transmission.


Outcome B: Overlapping clusters
G3 and G4 overlap substantially in shape space. Shape variation is continuous, not categorical.
Implication: The G3/G4 typological boundary may be a modern analytical construct rather than an emic (insider) category recognized by Bronze Age communities. Shape changed gradually, not in a discrete step.


Outcome C: Geographic gradient cuts across typological groups
PC axes that capture most variation correlate with geographic position, not with G3/G4 group membership.
Implication: Shape variation reflects local production traditions that don’t align with the typological sequence — regional craft identity was stronger than temporal change.
None of these outcomes is “right” or “wrong.” Each tells us something important about Bronze Age social and technological organization.

The Statistical Test

# Permutation MANOVA on EFA PCA scores
f_stat, p_val = permutation_manova(scores, labels, n_perm=999, n_pcs=8)

print(f"\nPermutation MANOVA (G3 vs G4):")
print(f"  F = {f_stat:.3f}")
print(f"  p = {p_val:.3f}")
print(f"  {'SIGNIFICANT' if p_val < 0.05 else 'NOT SIGNIFICANT'} at α = 0.05")

# Effect size: proportion of variance explained
r2 = f_stat / (f_stat + (len(labels) - 2))
print(f"  R² ≈ {r2:.3f} ({r2*100:.1f}% of variance explained by group)")


Interpreting Effect Size



R² value
Interpretation




< 0.05
Very small effect — groups barely differ


0.05–0.15
Small effect


0.15–0.35
Medium effect


> 0.35
Large effect — groups strongly differ



Even if the test is significant (p < 0.05), a small R² means groups differ reliably but not dramatically.

# This code was generated by Claude when asked:
# "Write a Python function to read a TPS file and return a numpy array
#  of shape (n_specimens, n_landmarks, 2)"

import numpy as np

def read_tps(filepath):
    """Read a TPS file and return landmarks as (n, p, 2) array."""
    specimens = []
    current_lms = []
    n_lm = 0

    with open(filepath, 'r') as f:
        for line in f:
            line = line.strip()
            if line.startswith('LM='):
                n_lm = int(line.split('=')[1])
                current_lms = []
            elif line.startswith('IMAGE=') or line.startswith('ID='):
                if len(current_lms) == n_lm and n_lm > 0:
                    specimens.append(current_lms)
            elif line and not line.startswith('SCALE=') and not line.startswith('CURVES='):
                try:
                    coords = list(map(float, line.split()))
                    if len(coords) == 2:
                        current_lms.append(coords)
                except:
                    pass

    # Add last specimen
    if len(current_lms) == n_lm and n_lm > 0:
        specimens.append(current_lms)

    return np.array(specimens)

title: Module 12: Big Questions + Course Synthesis
text:
What GM Cannot Do
Geometric morphometrics is a powerful tool, but it has real limits:

It only captures what you digitize. If the important variation is in surface texture, decoration, or color — shape analysis misses it entirely.
It requires comparable images. Poor photography, inconsistent orientation, or low resolution introduce error that can swamp real variation.
It does not explain. A significant group difference in shape space tells you that groups differ. It does not tell you why.
Small samples are risky. Permutation tests can detect large differences with small samples, but false discoveries are a real risk.
The landmark protocol is a hypothesis. The choice of which landmarks to place encodes assumptions about what variation matters. Different protocols can give different results on the same objects.

title: Module 12: Big Questions + Course Synthesis
text:
Reproducibility and Open Data
Science advances through reproducibility — the ability to check and extend each other’s work. Modern archaeology increasingly recognizes this. The most important practical habits:

Share your data. Upload your TPS files and metadata to Zenodo or OSF with a DOI.
Share your code. Post your Colab notebook publicly (or via GitHub).
Document your protocol. Write up your landmark placement rules clearly enough that someone else can replicate them.
Report effect sizes, not just p-values.

The datasets in this course (coins, axes) were made available by researchers who followed these principles. Future archaeologists will be able to re-analyze and extend this work.

title: Module 12: Big Questions + Course Synthesis
text:
3D Morphometrics: A Preview
The frontier of archaeological GM is three-dimensional analysis. Instead of a 2D outline or a set of 2D landmarks, 3D GM captures the full surface geometry of an object.

How 3D data is acquired:

Structured light scanning (Artec, NextEngine): fast, accurate, expensive
CT scanning: for complex internal shapes (lithic flaking, pottery walls)
Photogrammetry (Meshroom, Agisoft): free or cheap, requires 30–100 overlapping photos, works on any phone



Why 3D matters for archaeology:

A coin has depth — the relief of the portrait is 3D information we lose in 2D
An axe has two faces that may differ
A pot has a 3D surface, not just a profile

The auto3dgm package (used in our source course materials — see Morphometrics-course/auto3dgm_example.zip) automates 3D GPA without requiring manual landmark placement, using Minimum Description Length principles.
If you are interested in pursuing 3D GM for your final project or future research, speak with the instructor.

title: Module 11: Testing Hypotheses — Statistics in Shape Space
text:
Shape data from GM is multivariate: each specimen is described by many variables (PC scores, or raw Procrustes coordinates). Standard univariate tests (t-test, ANOVA) test one variable at a time. For shape, we need tests that work in many dimensions at once.
Furthermore, shape data does not always follow the assumptions of classical parametric tests (multivariate normality, equal variance). Sample sizes in archaeology are often small.
The solution used in modern GM: permutation-based tests.

title: Module 11: Testing Hypotheses — Statistics in Shape Space
text:
The Logic of Permutation Tests
A permutation test asks: how often would we see a difference this large (or larger) between groups if the group labels were just randomly assigned?

Step-by-step:

Calculate the observed test statistic (e.g., F-ratio comparing within-group to between-group variation)
Randomly permute the group labels among specimens, keeping the data fixed
Re-calculate the test statistic
Repeat steps 2–3 many times (999 or 9999 permutations)
The p-value = the proportion of permuted statistics ≥ the observed statistic

No distributional assumptions. Works with small samples. Widely accepted in the GM literature.

title: Module 11: Testing Hypotheses — Statistics in Shape Space
text:
MANOVA in Shape Space
MANOVA (Multivariate Analysis of Variance) tests whether group centroids (mean shapes) differ more than expected by chance.
In GM, we typically apply MANOVA to the first several PC scores (capturing, say, 90% of shape variance). This is what our permutation_manova() function does.
# Applied to any of our three datasets
f_stat, p_val = permutation_manova(scores, labels, n_perm=999, n_pcs=10)
r2 = f_stat / (f_stat + (len(labels) - 2))  # approx effect size

print(f"F = {f_stat:.3f}, p = {p_val:.3f}, R² = {r2:.3f}")

title: Module 11: Testing Hypotheses — Statistics in Shape Space
text:
Effect Size: R²
The p-value tells us whether groups differ. The effect size tells us how much they differ.
In GM, the standard effect size is R² — the proportion of total shape variance explained by group membership:
\[R^2 = \frac{SS_{between}}{SS_{total}}\]
An analysis can be statistically significant with a tiny R². For example: if p = 0.001 but R² = 0.04, groups differ reliably but the group difference accounts for only 4% of total shape variation. The other 96% is variation within groups.






Always report both p and R²



In archaeology, where sample sizes are often small and variation is high, R² is often more informative than the p-value alone.

title: Module 11: Testing Hypotheses — Statistics in Shape Space
text:
Allometry: When Size Predicts Shape
Allometry is the relationship between size and shape. In biology, larger organisms often have proportionally different shapes from smaller ones (think of how a puppy’s head looks different from an adult dog’s).
In archaeology: - Larger coins may have different portrait proportions than smaller ones - Larger pottery vessels may have proportionally narrower necks - Larger axes may have relatively wider blades
Testing allometry:
# Test: does centroid size predict shape?
from scipy.stats import pearsonr

# Correlate centroid sizes with PC1 scores
r, p = pearsonr(centroid_sizes, scores[:, 0])
print(f"Allometry (size vs. PC1): r = {r:.3f}, p = {p:.3f}")

# Scatter plot
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
plt.scatter(np.log(centroid_sizes), scores[:, 0], alpha=0.7)
plt.xlabel("Log centroid size")
plt.ylabel("PC1 score (shape)")
plt.title("Allometric plot: size vs. shape PC1")
# Add regression line
m, b = np.polyfit(np.log(centroid_sizes), scores[:, 0], 1)
x = np.linspace(np.log(centroid_sizes).min(), np.log(centroid_sizes).max(), 100)
plt.plot(x, m*x + b, 'r--')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
If allometry is significant: you may want to remove the size effect before comparing groups (using residuals from the allometric regression).

title: Module 11: Testing Hypotheses — Statistics in Shape Space
text:
Multiple Comparisons
If you are comparing 5 pottery periods against each other pairwise, you run 10 comparisons. By chance, you expect at least one to be “significant” at p < 0.05 — even if there is no real difference anywhere.
Solutions:

Bonferroni correction: divide your α threshold by the number of tests. For 10 tests, use p < 0.005 instead of p < 0.05.
Benjamini-Hochberg FDR: less conservative, controls the false discovery rate rather than the family-wise error rate.
A priori hypotheses: only test comparisons you predicted before looking at the data. This is the most principled approach.

from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests

p_values = [0.03, 0.04, 0.001, 0.08, 0.02]  # example: 5 pairwise tests
reject, p_corrected, _, _ = multipletests(p_values, method='bonferroni')

for orig, corr, rej in zip(p_values, p_corrected, reject):
    print(f"p = {orig:.3f} → corrected p = {corr:.3f} → {'SIGNIFICANT' if rej else 'ns'}")

title: Module 10: Case Study III — Pottery and Ceramic Traditions
text:
Pottery is the most ubiquitous artefact in archaeological sites almost everywhere in the world. It survives well, is highly sensitive to cultural traditions, and has been classified typologically for over a century. It is also the ideal object for outline analysis: vessel profiles are smooth curves with no discrete landmark points.
Pottery shape reflects: - Production technique — wheel-thrown vs. hand-built produces different profile shapes - Function — storage jars, cooking pots, and serving bowls have characteristic morphologies - Chronology — vessel forms changed over time in most traditions - Cultural identity — potters learned their craft within communities; shape encodes that transmission - Exchange — when pottery moved between communities, shapes were copied (and subtly transformed)
This week has two parts. First you read about a published case study. Then you run your own analysis on a real open-access dataset.

section: Part I — Published Case Study: Bibracte Celtic Ceramics
text:
Part I — Published Case Study: Bibracte Celtic Ceramics

What was the question?
Ceramic typology is built on the expert’s eye: an archaeologist looks at a vessel and assigns it to a type. But can a computer reach the same conclusion using shape alone? And if so, what does this tell us about whether typology captures real morphological structure?
This is the question that Wilczek et al. (2014) asked using 154 complete Iron Age vessels from Bibracte, a major Celtic oppidum (fortified town) in Burgundy, France. Bibracte was the capital of the Aedui tribe in the Second Iron Age (2nd century BC – 1st century AD) and is one of the most extensively excavated oppida in Europe.


The dataset
154 vessels with complete, well-preserved cross-sections. Assigned to 8 functional types by the traditional typology of Barral et al. (1995):

Outlines were extracted from published archaeological drawings (1200 dpi scans, external half cross-section mirrored to full profile), then processed by Elliptic Fourier Analysis (EFA) using 20 harmonics.


What they found






Key result (Wilczek et al. 2014)



PC1 captures ~93% of total shape variance. The main axis of shape variation is elongation: plates occupy one extreme (wide, flat) and bottles occupy the other (tall, narrow neck). Bowls, pots, cups, and goblets fall between these endpoints.
An unsupervised computer clustering of shape space (with no knowledge of the traditional types) produced 7 clusters that closely match the 8 traditional types — the computer and the archaeologist largely agreed. This validates that EFA captures the same morphological structure that typologists have described intuitively for decades.
Importantly, some types show high internal shape variation (pots, goblets) while others are tightly clustered (plates, bottles). This reveals which types are morphologically coherent and which may overlap functionally.




Why this matters
EFA makes typology reproducible and quantifiable. Anyone can run the same code on the same images and get the same result. The expert is still needed to interpret those results archaeologically — but the initial classification can be automated and tested statistically.
Citation: Wilczek, J., Monna, F., Barral, P., Burlet, L., Chateau, C., Navarro, N. (2014). Morphometrics of Second Iron Age ceramics — strengths, weaknesses, and comparison with traditional typology. Journal of Archaeological Science 50: 39–50. DOI: 10.1016/j.jas.2014.05.033

The research question
Not all shape questions are about typology. A different and equally important question is about production and selection:

Are jars from kiln sites (where they were made) more standardized in shape than jars from burial contexts (where families chose specific vessels to inter with the dead)?

If kiln-produced jars are highly uniform, that tells us something about production organization — potters working to a standard. If burial jars show different or more varied shapes, that might mean families selected visually distinctive vessels, or that different kilns supplied different markets.

The Pottery Pipeline






Open the Week 10 Notebook

This notebook is pre-built — run it cell by cell without writing any new code. Focus on interpretation.



Step 1 — Install and import
!pip install pyefd scikit-image --quiet

import os, zipfile, requests
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from PIL import Image
from skimage import measure
import pyefd
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu


Step 2 — Download and unpack the dataset
# Download from Zenodo (run once — ~30 MB)
url = "https://zenodo.org/records/15781166/files/Ogame_GMM.zip?download=1"
r = requests.get(url, stream=True)
with open("Ogame_GMM.zip", "wb") as f:
    for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):
        f.write(chunk)

with zipfile.ZipFile("Ogame_GMM.zip") as z:
    z.extractall(".")
print("Done. Files extracted to Ogame_GMM/")


Step 3 — Load metadata
samples = pd.read_csv("Ogame_GMM/Ogame_Samples.csv")
# Rename the long column for convenience
samples = samples.rename(columns={
    samples.columns[3]: "context_code"
})
samples["context"] = samples["context_code"].map({1: "Burial", 2: "Kiln"})
print(samples["context"].value_counts())
print(samples["Site Code"].value_counts())


Step 4 — Extract outlines and compute EFA
def extract_outline(image_path):
    """Extract the external outline of a black vessel silhouette on white background."""
    img = np.array(Image.open(image_path).convert('L'))
    binary = img < 128                         # True where vessel is (dark pixels)
    contours = measure.find_contours(binary.astype(float), 0.5)
    if not contours:
        return None
    return max(contours, key=len)              # largest contour = vessel outline

records = []
img_dir = "Ogame_GMM/Ogame_Profiles_All"

for _, row in samples.iterrows():
    path = os.path.join(img_dir, f"{row['Sample ID']}.png")
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        continue
    outline = extract_outline(path)
    if outline is None or len(outline) < 50:
        continue
    y, x = outline[:, 0], outline[:, 1]   # skimage returns (row, col)
    # Compute EFA with 20 harmonics, normalised for size and orientation
    coeffs = pyefd.elliptic_fourier_descriptors(
        np.column_stack([x, y]), order=20, normalize=True
    )
    records.append({
        "sample_id":  row["Sample ID"],
        "site_code":  row["Site Code"],
        "context":    row["context"],
        **{f"c{i:03d}": v for i, v in enumerate(coeffs.ravel())}
    })

df = pd.DataFrame(records)
print(f"Processed {len(df)} jars successfully")


Step 5 — PCA and visualisation
coeff_cols = [c for c in df.columns if c.startswith("c")]
X = df[coeff_cols].values

pca = PCA()
scores = pca.fit_transform(X)
var1 = pca.explained_variance_ratio_[0] * 100
var2 = pca.explained_variance_ratio_[1] * 100

# ── Plot 1: colour by depositional context ───────────────────────────────────
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6))

colors = {"Kiln": "#e07b39", "Burial": "#4a90c4"}
for ctx, col in colors.items():
    mask = df["context"] == ctx
    axes[0].scatter(scores[mask, 0], scores[mask, 1],
                    c=col, label=f"{ctx} (n={mask.sum()})",
                    s=50, alpha=0.75, edgecolors="white", linewidths=0.5)

axes[0].set_xlabel(f"PC1 ({var1:.1f}%)")
axes[0].set_ylabel(f"PC2 ({var2:.1f}%)")
axes[0].set_title("Ogame Jar Shape Space — by Depositional Context")
axes[0].axhline(0, color="grey", lw=0.5, ls="--")
axes[0].axvline(0, color="grey", lw=0.5, ls="--")
axes[0].legend()

# ── Plot 2: colour by production site (kiln sites only) ──────────────────────
kiln_mask = df["context"] == "Kiln"
kiln_sites = df.loc[kiln_mask, "site_code"].unique()
kiln_colors = {"FR": "#d62728", "KM": "#ff7f0e"}
for site in kiln_sites:
    mask = df["site_code"] == site
    axes[1].scatter(scores[mask, 0], scores[mask, 1],
                    c=kiln_colors.get(site, "#aaaaaa"),
                    label=f"{site} (n={mask.sum()})",
                    s=55, alpha=0.8, edgecolors="white", linewidths=0.5)

axes[1].set_xlabel(f"PC1 ({var1:.1f}%)")
axes[1].set_ylabel(f"PC2 ({var2:.1f}%)")
axes[1].set_title("Kiln Sites Compared — FR vs KM")
axes[1].axhline(0, color="grey", lw=0.5, ls="--")
axes[1].axvline(0, color="grey", lw=0.5, ls="--")
axes[1].legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("ogame_pca.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()
print(f"PC1: {var1:.1f}% | PC2: {var2:.1f}% | Together: {var1+var2:.1f}%")


Step 6 — Statistical test (kiln vs. burial)
pc1_kiln   = scores[df["context"] == "Kiln",   0]
pc1_burial = scores[df["context"] == "Burial",  0]

stat, p = mannwhitneyu(pc1_kiln, pc1_burial, alternative="two-sided")
print(f"Mann-Whitney U test on PC1 scores:")
print(f"  Kiln mean PC1:   {pc1_kiln.mean():.4f}")
print(f"  Burial mean PC1: {pc1_burial.mean():.4f}")
print(f"  U = {stat:.1f}, p = {p:.4f}")
if p < 0.05:
    print("  → Significant difference in shape between kiln and burial jars.")
else:
    print("  → No significant difference — shapes overlap.")

text:
Interpreting the Results
Work through these questions with your PCA plots:

Do kiln jars and burial jars separate in shape space? If yes, what does that mean archaeologically? If no — what might explain the lack of difference?
Do the two kiln sites (FR and KM) cluster separately? If yes, this suggests each workshop had its own production style. If they overlap, kilns were producing to a shared regional standard.
What shape features drive PC1? Look at jars plotted at the extreme left vs. extreme right of your scatter plot. Ask: what is visually different about those vessels?
What is the spread within each context? High variance in burial jars could mean families chose idiosyncratic vessels; low variance in kiln jars would suggest production standardization.
Connect to historical context: The Edo period (1600–1800) was a time of expanding commercial production in Kyushu. Large kilns like Furukameyashimo (FR) produced for regional markets. Did commercial production lead to more standardized jar forms than jars selected for burial?

# Mount Google Drive (run once per session)
from google.colab import drive

from google.colab import files
